Sabbath Day (Doctrine)
SAB-bath DAY
n. phrase
Hebrew shabbāt, from shābat (to cease, rest); the seventh day of the week, established at creation as the day of God’s rest from His work and given to Israel as the perpetual sign of the covenant.

Biblical Definition

The Sabbath day is one of the foundational structural categories of biblical theology, established at creation, codified in the Decalogue, central to Israel’s covenantal life, fulfilled and re-anchored in Christ, and continuing under the New Covenant in the Christian Lord’s Day. The doctrine has several structural moments. First, creation. Genesis 2:2-3: and on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made. And God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it: because that in it he had rested from all his work which God created and made. The Sabbath is grounded in the very order of creation, not merely in the Mosaic covenant; God Himself rested on the seventh day and sanctified it. Second, the Decalogue. Exodus 20:8-11 and Deuteronomy 5:12-15 set the fourth commandment: remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work: But the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God: in it thou shalt not do any work... The Sabbath is grounded in the work-and-rest pattern of God Himself (Exodus version) and in the redemption from Egyptian slavery (Deuteronomy version). Third, the Mosaic covenant detail. The Sabbath is the sign of the covenant between the LORD and Israel (Ex 31:13-17). Its violation is severe (Num 15:32-36). It is observed weekly, with cessation of ordinary labor for the household, servants, foreigners, and even animals (Ex 20:10). Fourth, the prophetic correction. The prophets repeatedly correct empty Sabbath-keeping (Isa 58:13-14) and condemn Sabbath-violation as covenant-breaking (Neh 13:15-22; Ezek 20). Fifth, the Christological fulfillment. Christ presents Himself as Lord even of the sabbath day (Mark 2:28); He corrects Pharisaic legalistic Sabbath-keeping; He performs healings on the Sabbath as proper works of mercy; He offers Himself as the One who gives true rest to the weary (come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest, Matt 11:28). Hebrews 4 develops the theology: there remains a sabbath-rest for the people of God; entering the rest is by faith, not by works; the rest is finally consummated in the eschatological rest with God. Sixth, the New Covenant transposition. After Christ’s resurrection, the church gathered on the first day of the week (the Lord’s Day, Sunday, the day of the resurrection) for worship and the breaking of bread (Acts 20:7; 1 Cor 16:2; Rev 1:10). The historic Reformed tradition has understood this as the transposition of the Sabbath from the seventh day to the first—the perpetual moral substance of the fourth commandment (one day in seven set apart for worship and rest, grounded in creation) carried forward, with the specific day shifted to commemorate the resurrection. Some Reformed and almost all Lutheran traditions have understood the matter more loosely (the ceremonial-specific Sabbath of the Mosaic covenant fulfilled in Christ, with the Lord’s Day kept as the appointed Christian day of worship without the strict Sabbatarian application). Either way, the Christian honors the Lord’s Day as the appointed day of worship, finds his ultimate Sabbath-rest in Christ, and awaits the consummate Sabbath-rest in the new heavens and earth.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SABBATH as the day which God appointed to be observed by the Jews as a day of rest from all secular labor or employment, and to be kept holy and consecrated to His service and worship; established at creation, codified in the Decalogue, fulfilled in Christ, transposed to the Lord’s Day under the New Covenant.

expand to see more

SABBATH, n. — 1. The day which God appointed to be observed by the Jews as a day of rest from all secular labor or employment, and to be kept holy and consecrated to His service and worship. 2. The day of the week appointed for the worship of God by Christians (the Lord’s Day or first day of the week); the Christian Sabbath. 3. Intermission of pain or sorrow; time of rest.

REST, n. — Cessation from motion or action of any kind; freedom from labor or exertion; in scripture, both the weekly rest of the Sabbath and the eschatological rest that remains for the people of God (Heb 4:9).

Key Scripture

Exodus 20:8-11 — "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work: But the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God: in it thou shalt not do any work..."

Mark 2:27-28 — "And he said unto them, The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath: Therefore the Son of man is Lord also of the sabbath."

Hebrews 4:9-10 — "There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God. For he that is entered into his rest, he also hath ceased from his own works, as God did from his."

Revelation 1:10 — "I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s day, and heard behind me a great voice, as of a trumpet."

Modern Corruption

The Sabbath doctrine is corrupted, on one side, by Sabbatarian over-rigor that has often loaded the day with prohibitions the New Testament does not warrant and missed the rest-in-Christ substance (the Pharisaic pattern Christ rebuked, repeated in some strict Reformed traditions)—and on the other by the general contemporary collapse of any meaningful Lord’s Day observance, with Sundays now largely indistinguishable from other days in the lives of most Christians.

expand to see more

Sabbatarian over-rigor has been a recurring corruption across both Jewish and Christian history. The Pharisaic pattern Christ rebuked—loading the Sabbath with hundreds of detailed prohibitions, treating the day as legal-test more than rest-and-worship, missing the day’s purpose for refreshment and mercy-works—has been repeated in some strict Reformed traditions that have produced households exhausted by Sabbath-rigor rather than rested by Sabbath-grace. Christ’s corrective stands: the sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath. The day is given for the worship of God and the refreshment of His people, not as a legalistic test loading the conscience with prohibitions. The recovery is the recovery of the day’s purpose—rest and worship in proper proportion—without the over-rigor that has often discredited Sabbath-keeping in the eyes of believers who experienced its legalistic distortion.

The opposite corruption is the general contemporary collapse of any meaningful Lord’s Day observance. Sundays in the lives of most contemporary believers are now largely indistinguishable from other days: church attendance for an hour or two, then back to ordinary work, shopping, entertainment, and the patterns of every other day. The structured one-day-in-seven set apart for worship and rest, which both Old and New Testament patterns assume, has been largely lost in most contemporary Christian practice. The cost is pastoral and personal: the believer who has no day-of-rest is the believer perpetually tired, perpetually distracted, perpetually without the structured worship-and-refreshment the Sabbath-pattern provides. The recovery is the recovery of Lord’s Day discipline: deliberate cessation from ordinary labor and commerce, deliberate prioritization of corporate worship, deliberate use of the day for spiritual refreshment, fellowship, family worship, and rest in Christ. The believer need not adopt strict Sabbatarian rigor (which can become its own bondage) to recover the substantial Lord’s Day pattern. The simple discipline of treating the Lord’s Day differently from the other days of the week—gathered worship as the day’s priority, ordinary commerce suspended, deliberate refreshment in the Lord and His people—restores much of what has been lost without the over-rigor that has discredited the doctrine.

Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shabbāt (Sabbath, rest), from shābat (to cease); Greek sabbaton; the seventh-day weekly rest established at creation, codified in the Decalogue, fulfilled in Christ as Lord of the Sabbath, and transposed under the New Covenant to the Lord’s Day (first day of the week) commemorating the resurrection.

expand to see more

Hebrew shabbāt (H7676) — Sabbath (over 100 OT uses).

Hebrew shābat (H7673) — to cease, rest (the verb).

Greek sabbaton (G4521) — Sabbath, week (68 NT uses).

Greek sabbatismos (G4520) — a sabbath-rest, sabbath-keeping (Heb 4:9).

"Hebrews 4:9 names a rest (sabbatismos) to the people of God as the ongoing substance behind the weekly observance, with its consummate fulfillment in eternal rest with God."

"Sabbatarian over-rigor produces exhausted Pharisaic households missing the day’s grace; contemporary collapse loses any meaningful Lord’s Day distinction; biblical pattern is one-day-in-seven set apart for worship and rest, refreshing and Christ-centered."
